newsitem.title: USA: Grain exporters skeptical of fresh Russian demand.
newsitem.headline: Grain exporters skeptical of fresh Russian demand.

text.p: American grain export traders said they have seen no indication of fresh Russian interest in buying U.S. corn and soymeal and were skeptical that new business with Russia would develop any time soon.
"We're not seeing any interest, not at all," one exporter said. "Quite frankly, nobody in the industry expects much interest from them at the moment."

Traders cited problems with financing purchases as a major stumbling block to any fresh business with Russia. "There is such political turmoil in that country that you cannot get a straight answer out of anybody," a second exporter said.

In a speech in St Petersburg Tuesday, Russian Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun said he expects Russia to import 4.0 to 4.5 million tonnes of feedgrains, mostly corn and soymeal, this year from the United States, Canada and Australia, up from three to four million tonnes expected earlier.
He cited heavy rains in Siberia as possibly hurting crops.
"They (Russia) have not paid their farmers for the grain that has been sold to the government," the second exporter said. "For them to import they first have to pay back debt to farmers."

"There are occasions when we hear from them and they nibble for 20,000 or 80,000 tonnes of corn or meal. But it never happens because they end up buying from some eastern European country where they rail it in," the exporter said.

"So they do inquire on occasion but I have not heard anything from them in months. There was a lot of conversation when Boris Yeltsin got elected that they were going to buy. But buy what? We have been hearing this for two years."
The exporter said recent IMF funding for Russia -- a $10 billion IMF loan approved in March, based on Russia meeting economic targets -- was only a psychological boost.
"Nobody sells them anything because they are so fearful they won't get paid. People would want assurances from our government to back the contract," the exporter said.
"I do not think it is impossible, but I think the average grain trader will say, 'Yeah, right. I'll believe it when I see it,'" the exporter said.
Exporters said Russia has raised meat, not grain, imports.

"They have been tightening their belts in buying processed beef and processed products instead of the grain because they do not have the infrastructure anymore to process the animals," the second exporter said.
A third exporter also expressed doubts.
"Those numbers (4.0 to 4.5 million tonnes of grain) are not out of line for what they are capable of importing. I have not seen any interest so far," the exporter said.

However, the exporter said, the talk "is probably stemming from some politically based conversations. It is no different from (U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan) Glickman saying we intend to ship a lot of poultry around the world."
